---
title: "Analysis of Variance"
---



## Learning Objectives

1. Know when to use analysis of variance
2. Understand that the null hypothesis for analysis of variance is no difference in means across groups or values of explanatory variables
3. Understand how to decompose variance into its sources
4. Understand the problem of multiple hypothesis testing

# To the board...



## [Analysis of variance]{.alert}: do the group means differ?

::: {.columns style="align-items: center;"}
::: {.column width="45%"}
Is the mean of $Y$ the same in every group?

A small example: three groups, five observations each

::: {.fragment}
ANOVA splits the variation in $Y$ into two sources: variation [among]{.alert} the group means and variation [within]{.alert} the groups
:::
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](12-anova-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){fig-align='center' width=5in}
:::
:::

:::
:::

## Sum of squares: $SS_Y$ {.top-align}

::: columns
::: {.column width="45%"}
$$
SS_Y = \sum (Y_i - \overline{Y})^2
$$

The total variation in $Y$: how far every observation is from the overall mean, $\overline{Y}$
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](12-anova-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){fig-align='center' width=5in}
:::
:::

:::
:::

## Sum of squares: $SS_{group}$ {.top-align}

::: columns
::: {.column width="45%"}
$$
SS_{group} = \sum n_j (\hat{Y}_j - \overline{Y})^2
$$

::: {.incremental}
- $\hat{Y}_j$ is the mean of group $j$: the prediction for every observation in that group
- $n_j$ is the number of observations in group $j$
:::

::: {.fragment}
$SS_{group}$ is [big]{.alert} when the group means are far from $\overline{Y}$
:::
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](12-anova-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){fig-align='center' width=5in}
:::
:::

:::
:::

## Sum of squares: $SS_{error}$ {.top-align}

::: columns
::: {.column width="45%"}
$$
SS_{error} = \sum (Y_i - \hat{Y}_j)^2
$$

Compare each data point to the mean of its [own group]{.alert}

::: {.fragment}
The variation within groups: what the groups do not explain
:::
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](12-anova-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){fig-align='center' width=5in}
:::
:::

:::
:::

## Sum of squares: all together

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
::: columns
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.fragment}
$SS_Y$ $=$


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](12-anova-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){fig-align='center' width=3.2in}
:::
:::


$\sum (Y_i - \overline{Y})^2$
:::
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.fragment}
$SS_{group}$ $+$


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](12-anova-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){fig-align='center' width=3.2in}
:::
:::


$\sum n_j (\hat{Y}_j - \overline{Y})^2$
:::
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.fragment}
$SS_{error}$


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](12-anova-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){fig-align='center' width=3.2in}
:::
:::


$\sum (Y_i - \hat{Y}_j)^2$
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Mean squares

A sum of squares gets bigger with every data point we add, so we divide by the degrees of freedom to get a [mean square]{.alert}

$$
MS_{group} = \frac{SS_{group}}{df_{group}} \qquad\qquad MS_{error} = \frac{SS_{error}}{df_{error}}
$$

::: {.incremental}
- $df_{group} = (\text{number of groups}) - 1$
- $df_{error} = N - (\text{number of groups})$: we estimate one mean for each group
:::

::: {.fragment}
In our example, 3 groups and $N =$ 15: $df_{group} =$ 2 and $df_{error} =$ 12
:::

## Sum of squares and mean squares in *R*


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
y_bar <- mean(small_data$y)
group_mean <- ave(small_data$y, small_data$group)

ss_y <- sum((small_data$y - y_bar) ^ 2)
ss_group <- sum((group_mean - y_bar) ^ 2)
ss_error <- sum((small_data$y - group_mean) ^ 2)

ss_y
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 16.98
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
ss_group + ss_error
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 16.98
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
ms_group <- ss_group / (3 - 1)
ms_error <- ss_error / (15 - 3)

ms_group
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 7.2
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
ms_error
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.215
```


:::
:::


## Comparing $MS_{group}$ to $MS_{error}$


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](12-anova-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){fig-align='center' width=10in}
:::
:::


::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.fragment}
The group means are far apart compared to the spread within each group
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.fragment}
The group means are close together compared to the spread within each group
:::
:::
:::

## $F$-statistic {.top-align}

$$
F = \frac{MS_{group}}{MS_{error}}
$$

::: {style="margin-top: -0.6em;"}
How much more variation between groups ($MS_{group}$) compared to variation in "residuals" ($MS_{error}$), bounded $[0, \infty)$
:::


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](12-anova-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){fig-align='center' width=8.8in}
:::
:::


## The null hypothesis

::: {.incremental}
- $H_0$: $\mu_A = \mu_B = \mu_C$, all of the group means are equal
- $H_A$: not all of the means are equal
:::

::: {.fragment}
For any number of groups, $k$: $H_0$: $\mu_1 = \mu_2 = \dots = \mu_k$
:::

::: {.fragment}
If $H_0$ is true, $MS_{group}$ and $MS_{error}$ both estimate the variation within groups, so $F \approx 1$
:::

::: {.fragment}
If some means differ, $MS_{group}$ gets bigger than $MS_{error}$ and $F$ gets big
:::

## Null hypothesis test with $F$

If $H_0$ is true, $F$ follows an [F-distribution]{.alert} with $df_{group}$ and $df_{error}$ degrees of freedom

::: {.columns style="align-items: center;"}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.fragment}

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](12-anova-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){fig-align='center' width=4.6in}
:::
:::


$F_{2,12} =$ 0.55, $P =$ 0.59

$df_{group} =$ 2, $df_{error} =$ 12
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.fragment}

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](12-anova-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){fig-align='center' width=4.6in}
:::
:::


$F_{2,12} =$ 33.5, $P =$ $1.2 \times 10^{-5}$

$df_{group} =$ 2, $df_{error} =$ 12
:::
:::
:::

## Null hypothesis test with $F$

The [P-value]{.alert} is the probability of an $F$ at least as big as the observed $F$, if $H_0$ is true

::: {.fragment}
If $P \leq 0.05$: reject $H_0$

If $P > 0.05$: fail to reject $H_0$
:::

::: {.fragment}
If we reject $H_0$: at least one group mean is different from the others
:::

## Finding $F$ and the P-value in *R*


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
f_stat <- ms_group / ms_error
f_stat
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 33.48837
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
pf(q = f_stat, df1 = 3 - 1, df2 = 15 - 3, lower.tail = FALSE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 1.23053e-05
```


:::
:::


::: {.fragment}
`q` is our $F$ statistic, `df1` is $df_{group}$, `df2` is $df_{error}$

$P < 0.05$, so we reject $H_0$: at least one group mean is different from the others
:::

## Example ANOVA for multiple groups in *R*


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# make some pretend data
groups <- rep(LETTERS[1:3], each = 10)
y <- 1.2 * as.numeric(as.factor(groups)) + rnorm(30, mean = 0, sd = 0.5)

dat_groups <- data.frame(group = groups, y = y)

head(dat_groups, n = 3)
```

## Assumptions of ANOVA for groups

- Random and independent samples
- Normal distribution for each group
- Equal variances within each group

## What to do if assumptions are not met?

- Do ANOVA anyway (if deviations are minor)
- Transform
- More advanced stats

## Interpreting ANOVA for groups

ANOVA does not tell you which group(s) is/are different!  Just that a difference exists


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](12-anova-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){fig-align='center' width=5in}
:::
:::


## Interpreting ANOVA for groups

If we want to know which groups are different, we need to do a "post hoc" test

- Post hoc tests are designed to account for multiple comparisons
- What are multiple comparisons and why can't we just do multiple $t$-tests?

## Pos hoc tests and multiple comparisons

Which groups are different?  Just do $t$-tests between all pairwise comparisons, right?

- The problem: doing multiple $t$-tests leads to a false positive rate $> \alpha$
- If we do 3 pairwise comparisons with $t$-tests and $\alpha = 0.05$ for each one, then probability of at least 1 false positive is:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
prob_false_positive <- 1 - dbinom(0, size = 3, prob = 0.05)
prob_false_positive
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.142625
```


:::
:::


## Pos hoc tests and multiple comparisons


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
prob_false_positive <- 1 - dbinom(0, size = 3, prob = 0.05)
prob_false_positive
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.142625
```


:::
:::


Each $t$-test is like a coin toss with "heads = false positive", the more you do, the more likely you'll get at least one "heads = false positive"

## Pos hoc tests and multiple comparisons

So we use a post hoc test:


::: {.cell}

:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# annoying, but we have to pass the model through the `aov` function
aov_group <- aov(mod_group)

# "Tukey Honest Significant Difference"
TukeyHSD(aov_group)
```
:::


## Pos hoc tests and multiple comparisons

So we use a post hoc test:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# "Tukey Honest Significant Difference"
TukeyHSD(aov_group)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
  Tukey multiple comparisons of means
    95% family-wise confidence level

Fit: aov(formula = mod_group)

$group
         diff       lwr      upr     p adj
B-A 0.9728723 0.4168185 1.528926 0.0005128
C-A 2.2447992 1.6887454 2.800853 0.0000000
C-B 1.2719269 0.7158731 1.827981 0.0000147
```


:::
:::


## Pos hoc tests and multiple comparisons

The adjusted Confidence Intervals and $P$-values make sure that the overall $\alpha$ remains at the desired level, usually 0.05

# Multi-factor ANOVA

## Learning Objectives

1. What is a multi-factor ANOVA, when do you use it, and how?

## A motivating (hypothetical) example

**fish biomass responding to restoration efforts in high and low impact areas**

::: {.incremental}
- Restoration was carried out at some sites along a coast
- Similar sites were left alone as controls
- Restoration and control sites were situated in areas of low and high human impact
:::

::: {.fragment}
[Question]{.alert}: does restoration increase fish biomass, and does it work as well where human impact is high as where it is low?
:::



## A motivating (hypothetical) example: sampling sites


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](12-anova-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){fig-align='center' width=8.5in}
:::
:::


*A cartoon map, not real locations: 15 sites for each combination of restoration and human impact*

## Two explanatory variables

::: {.no-bold-header}
|  | Low impact | High impact |
|:---|:---:|:---:|
| **Restored** | 15 sites | 15 sites |
| **Control** | 15 sites | 15 sites |
:::

::: {.incremental}
- [Response]{.alert}: fish biomass
- [Explanatory variables]{.alert}: restoration (restored or control) and human impact (low or high)
:::

::: {.fragment}
Every combination of the two factors (explanatory variables) is sampled
:::

## Multi-factor ANOVA: a question for each factor

::: {.incremental}
- Restoration: $H_0$: $\mu_{restored} = \mu_{control}$
- Human impact: $H_0$: $\mu_{low} = \mu_{high}$
:::

::: {.fragment}
Each factor is compared across the levels of the other factor, and gets its own $F$-test

$$
F = \frac{MS_{factor}}{MS_{error}}
$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
A third question: does the effect of restoration [depend on]{.alert} human impact? We'll get to this [interaction]{.alert} soon
:::

## Partitioning variation with two factors

$$
SS_Y = SS_{impact} + SS_{restoration} + SS_{error}
$$

::: {.incremental}
- Each factor's sum of squares measures how far its group means are from the overall mean, $\overline{Y}$
- $SS_{error}$ is the variation left over within each combination of the factors
:::

::: {.fragment}
With an interaction there is one more piece

$$
SS_Y = SS_{impact} + SS_{restoration} + SS_{impact \times restoration} + SS_{error}
$$
:::

## Example multi-factor ANOVA in *R*


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# make some pretend data
restoration <- factor(rep(c("restored", "control"), each = 30))
impact <- factor(rep(c("low", "high"), 30),
                 levels = c("low", "high"))

# compute expected response
fish_biomass <- -1 * as.numeric(impact) + 3 * as.numeric(restoration) -
  1 * as.numeric(impact) * as.numeric(restoration)

# add some noise
set.seed(123)
fish_biomass <- fish_biomass + rnorm(60, mean = 0, sd = 1)

dat <- data.frame(restoration, impact, fish_biomass)
```
:::


## Example multi-factor ANOVA in *R*


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
  restoration impact fish_biomass
1    restored    low   2.43952435
2    restored   high  -0.23017749
3    restored    low   4.55870831
4    restored   high   0.07050839
5    restored    low   3.12928774
6    restored   high   1.71506499
```


:::
:::


## Example multi-factor ANOVA in *R*


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(dat, aes(x = restoration, y = fish_biomass,
                fill = impact)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "YlGnBu", direction = -1)
```
:::


## Example multi-factor ANOVA in *R*


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](12-anova-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-28-1.png){fig-align='center' width=5in}

## Example multi-factor ANOVA in *R*


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mod <- lm(fish_biomass ~ impact + restoration, data = dat)
anova(mod)
```

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
